discoveries.headline: How a fake job interview opened Binance
discoveries.why: Binance says hackers stole $6.3 billion after compromising three software engineers' computers, one through a tampered tool found via a search ad and another through a fake job interview with the 'CEO' of a company that didn't exist. The FBI has blamed a North Korean hacking group, which North Korea rejects, and Binance says it is repaying every customer whose funds were taken. A sharp reminder that crypto security often comes down to people, not code. Education, not advice.

discoveries.headline: Six Brookings experts on Trump, Xi and Putin
discoveries.why: As the 33rd APEC Leaders' Meeting wraps up in Shenzhen, six Brookings scholars, including Ryan Hass, Yun Sun and Constanze Stelzenmüller, each take a question on what the meetings could mean. They cover the US-China trade truce, which would be extended by two months until January 2027, Europe's view and the possible three-way meeting with Putin. A deeper read to set alongside today's headlines.
discoveries.meta_credit: Brookings · Jonathan A. Czin, Kyle Chan, Ryan Hass, Scott M. Moore, Constanze Stelzenmüller and Yun Sun

discoveries.headline: A water lily and its ice twin win
discoveries.why: Finnish photographer Hannu Ahonen has taken the overall title in Nature Photographer of the Year 2026 with 'The One that Left and the One that Stayed': a lily leaf beside a sheet of ice in exactly its shape. The contest drew a record 27,108 entries from more than 96 countries. Scroll on for Audun Rikardsen's 'A Seal's Worst Nightmare' and Xuzhong Liu's 'Peach Blossoms in the Snow'.
discoveries.meta_credit: DIY Photography · Dunja Đuđić Kalinin · Nature Photographer of the Year

discoveries.headline: Five minutes with your breath
discoveries.why: Diana Winston, director of UCLA Mindful, recorded this short breathing meditation as part of a free library from UCLA Health. It takes five minutes, and the same page offers a 3-minute body scan, a loving-kindness practice and a body scan for sleep, each with a transcript. A calm place to start the day.

discoveries.headline: Anthropic gives its Agent Skills away
discoveries.why: A skill is simply a folder with a SKILL.md file that teaches an AI agent how to do a specific task, plus any scripts or notes it needs. Anthropic has now donated the Agent Skills standard, with its name, logo and agentskills.io, to the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, which it co-founded with Block and OpenAI. More than 70 platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor and VS Code, already use skills: agents learn everyday know-how one skill at a time, and the rulebook now belongs to everyone.

discoveries.headline: Ecca Vandal wins the Australian Music Prize
discoveries.why: Ecca Vandal has won the 22nd Australian Music Prize and its $50,000 first prize for LOOKING FOR PEOPLE TO UNFOLLOW, her second album and her first in nine years. She topped a shortlist that included Courtney Barnett, Julia Jacklin, Genesis Owusu and Baker Boy, from more than 600 albums considered. Put the record on and back an artist who took her time.
discoveries.meta_credit: Noise11 · Paul Cashmere · Australian Music Prize

discoveries.headline: Why we age, with Steve Austad
discoveries.why: Biologist Steve Austad of the University of Alabama at Birmingham has spent a career asking why some animals live far longer than others. On Big Biology he walks through the big theories of ageing, what long-lived animals like bats can teach us, and whether treatments could extend healthy life without costly trade-offs. A thoughtful listen for the commute. General information, not medical advice.

discoveries.headline: A 50-minute vinyasa flow
discoveries.why: In this free NHS Fitness Studio class, instructor LJ links breath and movement in a vinyasa flow she describes as 'meditation in motion', building strength, flexibility and steady breathing. It suits most people in good health with a reasonable level of fitness. Roll out a mat, keep a towel and water nearby, and give yourself the full session.

discoveries.headline: Strength and power, for midlife and beyond
discoveries.why: Stanford Lifestyle Medicine explains why women need both strength, the ability to resist force, and power, the ability to produce it quickly, which often fades faster with age, especially after menopause. Physical therapist and researcher Corey Rovzar suggests building strength first with squats, rows and step-ups, then adding power moves like fast squats and medicine ball passes. Practical rituals for staying strong for decades.
discoveries.meta_credit: Stanford Lifestyle Medicine · Anya Higashionna and Sharon Brock · Corey Rovzar
